fact: Most oral drugs are broken down in the liver by CYP enzymes. CYP3A4 handles about half of all drugs, so a new drug cleared by CYP3A4 can interact with common medicines that block it (for example clarithromycin, ketoconazole, grapefruit juice) and reach much higher blood levels.
Patients with liver impairment (Child-Pugh B or C) clear liver-metabolised drugs more slowly, often giving 2 to 3 times higher exposure. They need lower doses or exclusion until studied.
Drugs taken at high daily doses (above about 100 mg per day) that are mainly cleared by the liver carry a higher risk of drug-induced liver injury than low-dose drugs.
Kidney function falls with age; many people over 75 have about half the kidney clearance of a young adult. Drugs cleared by the kidney need dose adjustment based on creatinine clearance.

Blocking the hERG potassium channel in the heart lengthens the QT interval and can cause a dangerous arrhythmia (torsades de pointes). Lipophilic molecules with a basic amine group are the most common hERG blockers. Risk adds up with other QT-prolonging drugs such as ondansetron.
Low potassium or magnesium in the blood, and age over 65, increase the risk of QT-related arrhythmia.
Sulfonamide (sulfa) groups in a molecule can cause allergic skin reactions, rarely severe ones (Stevens-Johnson syndrome). People with a known sulfa allergy are at higher risk.
Polysorbate 80 and Cremophor (castor oil) used as solubilisers in IV formulations can trigger infusion and hypersensitivity reactions, usually within the first minutes of the first infusion.

People with G6PD deficiency (common in parts of South Asia, Africa and the Mediterranean) can have red blood cells destroyed (haemolysis) by oxidising drugs, including some sulfonamides and primaquine-like structures.
Most small-molecule drugs cross the placenta. New drugs without animal reproductive-toxicity data must exclude pregnant people and require contraception.
A high-fat meal can raise the absorption of poorly water-soluble oral drugs by 50 percent or more. The protocol must state whether the drug is taken fasting or with food.
Lactose is a common tablet filler; it is safe for most people but can cause symptoms in severe lactose intolerance. Propylene glycol in liquid formulations can be toxic to infants and young children.
Small, lipophilic molecules cross the blood-brain barrier more easily and are more likely to cause dizziness, sleepiness or confusion, especially in older adults.

In first-in-human studies, giving the first dose to one sentinel participant and waiting 24 to 48 hours before dosing the rest of the group prevents several people being harmed at once by an unexpected reaction.
